name: Mouth tape

lead: Mouth taping means placing a strip of gentle tape over the lips at night to keep the mouth closed and encourage nasal breathing. Social media credits it with better sleep, less snoring, fresher breath and less dry mouth, and some forums link it to a better jawline.

Sealing the lips sends air through the nose, which filters and humidifies it and may reduce dry mouth, and better sleep can mean a less puffy, fresher-looking face. A 2025 systematic review found ten studies with 213 patients, with two reporting significant improvement in sleep apnea markers. The reviews looked at sleep and breathing outcomes, not facial shape.

paras: Users apply a strip or porous patch across the lips just before sleep and peel it off in the morning, usually after starting with short trial runs while awake. People often pair it with nasal strips or saline rinses.

The main concerns are taping over nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep apnea, skin irritation and feeling suffocated. Clinicians advise that people with snoring, daytime sleepiness or blocked nasal airways be evaluated first. Claims of adult facial-bone change from breathing route are unsupported.

social.title: Mouth taping may help with snoring and sleep apnea
Mouth Taping for Sleep: Does It Work? (2025)

angle.text: Users tape their mouths at night to push nasal breathing, aiming for better sleep, fresher breath and a less puffy morning face. Reviews have examined sleep and snoring, and they did not assess facial shape.

lead: Mouth taping is the practice of placing a strip of tape, a porous patch or a similar adhesive over the lips during sleep to keep the mouth closed and encourage breathing through the nose. In looksmaxxing circles it is used as a low-cost routine to support nasal breathing and a closed-mouth posture, which proponents link to a tidier lower face, less dry mouth, fresher breath and less puffy-looking sleep, and it is often paired with tongue posture work or nasal care.[1][2][3][4]

The practice spread through social media in the 2020s, where it has been credited with better sleep, less snoring, fresher breath, and improved immunity, dental health and energy.[1][3] A November 2022 New York Times article on whether a piece of tape can help sleep is among the mainstream pieces Wikipedia cites as part of its rise.[3]

Published research is small. A 2025 systematic review located ten studies with 213 patients in total and found that two reported statistically significant improvement in sleep apnea markers, while others found no difference.[5] A scoping review found nine eligible studies and likewise noted that only two reported significant improvements in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) metrics.[1] A 2025 randomised crossover trial in 62 CPAP users found longer nightly CPAP use with silicone tape.[6] Authors of these reviews and commentaries call for more rigorous trials and discuss safety, particularly for people with nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep-disordered breathing.[5][1][7][8]

On facial structure, the clinical studies evaluated sleep and breathing outcomes and none assessed adult facial shape. The idea that chronic mouth breathing can influence face growth in children is described in the mouth breathing literature, and looksmaxxing communities extend it to adults, sometimes jokingly.[9][10]
infobox: Adhesive tape or porous patch over the lips

paras: Products range from household surgical tape to purpose-made strips and porous patches designed to sit over the lips. Wikipedia describes the practice as keeping the lips shut with a strip of surgical tape to prevent mouth breathing in sleep.[3] The practice is separate from medical uses of tape or chin straps in sleep clinics, although some clinical studies have used tape to test the effect of enforced nasal breathing.[5][11][12]

A 2015 pilot study cited by Wikipedia used novel porous oral patches rather than tape in patients with mild sleep apnea who breathed through the mouth, and the 2025 CPAP trial used silicone hypoallergenic tape.[3][6] Mouth tape is usually worn for the night and removed on waking.

Wikipedia gives no inventor or start date for mouth taping and says it gained popularity through social media in the 2020s; its main cited source is the 2022 New York Times article by Dani Blum.[3] A scoping review published in the American Journal of Otolaryngology analysed the first fifty eligible TikTok videos using the term and catalogued the claims made, finding better sleep and oral health the most common, along with the type of person presenting them.[1]

Clinicians noticed the trend. A 2023 letter in the British Dental Journal addressed it from a dental viewpoint, a 2024 editorial in The Journal of Physiology discussed it, and a JAMA Otolaryngology commentary asked whether mouth taping and sleep apnea therapies should be regulated.[13][7][8] The topic sits close to mewing and orthotropics, which Wikipedia says drew wide attention from 2019 and is linked in coverage to looksmaxxing subcultures, though that article does not itself describe mouth taping.[14]

sections.h: How it is proposed to work
paras: Proponents say sealing the lips forces air through the nose, which filters, warms and humidifies it. Wikipedia notes that nasal sinuses produce nitric oxide, which it says can help lower blood pressure and improve blood flow, and describes nasal breathing as allowing fuller breaths and helping the body relax.[3] Mouth breathing, by comparison, is associated with drying of the mouth in sleep, which can contribute to dental damage, bad breath, hoarseness and dry lips.[3][10]

A small randomised crossover experiment in eight healthy adults found that mouth-taped nasal breathing over two hours increased oral mucosal wetness, whereas mouth-only breathing with a nose clip nearly abolished it; the work also examined the surface tension of upper-airway lining liquid, which has been linked to airway collapsibility.[12]

Wikipedia's mouth breathing article reports that about 85 percent of cases are an adaptation to nasal congestion, and that chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face described as long face syndrome, though the relationship may also run in the other direction.[10] Proponents of mouth taping draw on this literature when they discuss facial effects.

On looksmax.org, mouth taping is discussed both as a way to promote nasal breathing and jaw development and, by some users, as a sleep aid only; one thread title calls it "cope" for facial change and says it is "for sleep."[15] A thread whose author claims forward growth of the maxilla and chin from nightly tape is partly tongue-in-cheek, with replies joking in kind.[9] Other users ask about skin irritation from the adhesive and about pairing tape with nasal sprays and a sleep apnea check when the nose is blocked.[2][16]

On T Nation, posters mention it in the context of snoring and sleep, and one user reports a first night that left him well rested.[17] The practice is commonly combined in these communities with tongue posture, nasal sprays, sleeping position and weight management, all aimed at nasal breathing and a defined lower face.

A 2022 preliminary study of 20 mouth-breathers with mild OSA taped the mouth with 3M hypoallergenic tape and repeated a home sleep test one week later; 13 (65 percent) met the responder definition of a 50 percent drop in snoring index, and the median apnea-hypopnea index fell from 8.3 to 4.7 events per hour (p = 0.0002), with the lowest oxygen saturation rising from 82.5 to 87 percent.[18] The authors suggested taping may be an alternative to CPAP or surgery for mild OSA, a conclusion the later systematic review did not adopt.[18][5]

A two-night home sleep test study of 71 participants examined mouth puffing and whether taping altered the oxygen desaturation index.[19] The 2025 systematic review in PLoS One pooled ten studies of 213 patients: two showed significant improvement in markers such as the apnea-hypopnea index or oxygen desaturations, others found no benefit, and many excluded patients with nasal obstruction or pathology.[5] A 2025 scoping review of nine studies found two with significant OSA improvements (one with tape alone, one with tape plus a mandibular advancement device), one in non-OSA patients showing less snoring with tape combined with other measures, one asthma study showing no benefit, and one showing less mouth leak during bilevel ventilation.[1]

In patients already using CPAP, a randomised crossover trial of 62 people with OSA found that silicone hypoallergenic mouth tape increased average CPAP use by about 52 minutes per night (95% CI 33 to 70) compared with no tape, with participants also reporting less daytime sleepiness, less snoring and less dry mouth.[6] A 2009 randomised single-blind crossover study examined overnight taping and asthma control.[20] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis examined nasal obstruction and mouth taping in relation to sleep apnea indicators.[11]
None of the cited studies tested whether mouth taping changes adult facial or jaw structure.

The 2025 systematic review concluded that indiscriminate mouth taping carries a potentially serious risk of harm, noting that studies not finding benefit raised risks such as asphyxiation in the presence of nasal obstruction, and called for more research on any clinical benefit.[5] Commentators have discussed taping over a blocked nose or in someone with untreated sleep apnea, as well as skin irritation from adhesive.[5][7][8]

Dr. Brian Chen, a paediatric sleep medicine specialist at Cleveland Clinic, lists difficulty breathing, lip and skin irritation, anxiety and trouble sleeping among risks, and says people with nasal obstruction, chronic allergies, sinus infections, enlarged tonsils, a deviated septum or heart problems should not use it; he suggests talking to a doctor first.[4] Wikipedia likewise notes that deviated septum, allergies, sinusitis and chronic congestion can make taping impractical.[3] Clinical authors recommend evaluation of persistent snoring, daytime sleepiness or nasal obstruction.[5][11][4]

A small body of human research exists. Two systematic reviews and a scoping review identified nine to ten eligible studies, two of which found significant improvements in OSA metrics.[5][1] A preliminary study of 20 mouth-breathers with mild OSA[18] and a two-night home sleep study of 71 participants[19] tested taping directly. A randomised crossover trial in 62 CPAP users found longer nightly CPAP use with mouth tape.[6] A trial in eight healthy subjects measured mucosal wetness and airway lining liquid surface tension.[12] A randomised single-blind crossover study examined asthma control.[20] A meta-analysis of nasal obstruction examined apnea-hypopnea index.[11] Reviewers describe the overall evidence as limited, and no study has examined facial structure outcomes.[5][1]

Related practices include nasal strips and dilators, nasal sprays, saline rinses, chin straps in clinical settings, myofunctional therapy and tongue posture work, and mewing, which Wikipedia associates with John Mew and Mike Mew and says is not supported by credible scientific research in the orthodontic literature.[14] Clinicians quoted by Cleveland Clinic also mention side sleeping, nasal strips, decongestants, CPAP and oral appliances as alternatives for snoring and sleep apnea.[4]
